title: Anne Ouyang (@anneouyang)
summary:
GPU Bourgeoisie: have the financial capacity to invest in a large quantity of high-performance GPUs and leverage them to advance ML projects. might even have substantial control over the distribution and availability of GPUs.
GPU Proletariat: rely on the availability of GPU resources to do ML projects but does not have ownership and control over them. access to GPUs often dependent on the support of the others
GPU Petit Bourgeoisie: have some access to GPU resources but limited compared to the GPU Bourgeoisie. Might own or rent a small number of GPUs but do not have extensive influence
GPU Lumpenproletariat: on the fringes of the ML community with irregular access to GPUs. Might resort to unconventional methods such as using cloud services with low availability or outdated hardware
GPU Aristocracy: have an extraordinary abundance of GPU resources that enable resource-intensive and often pioneering ML projects.

title: Anne Ouyang (@anneouyang)
summary:
I’m not anti-ideology, I think orgs and ideology can be great, just not this one. A heuristic for a good ideology could be “people you don’t admire becoming more admirable, and those you do becoming especially so” as a result of the ideology.
The ai safety researchers I look up to were compassionate and brilliant and intended to produce good outcomes before any ideology and EA mostly weighs them down with burden and guilt. Conversely, I don’t see a lot of non-compassionate and non-brilliant people pivoting and becoming great ai safety researchers bc of EA.
While I do think EA-thinking and spreadsheets are helpful for “where should I donate money this year” type decisions, I haven’t seen the “Sci-fi EA” longtermist thinking making most EAs more admirable. Usually it makes their thinking less clear, favors the ignoring of important nuances, and leads to bizarre outcomes for them and those around them. In theory lowering confidences and getting all the bayesian hygiene right should handle this, but in my experience in practice even trying to extrapolate so far with this specific framework tends to be poisonous

title: Anne Ouyang (@anneouyang)
summary:
AI as AI compiler?
Very excited to release KernelBench, a new code generation benchmark for evaluating models' ability to generate correct and efficient CUDA kernels.
KernelBench has 4 levels:
Level 1 (100 tasks): Single-kernel operators (e.g. matmuls)
Level 2 (100 tasks): Simple fusion patterns (e.g. conv + bias + ReLU)
Level 3 (50 tasks): Full architectures (e.g. MobileNet)
Level 4 (20 additional aspirational tasks): Huggingface architectures that require browsing the HF source code and making changes to the library.

title: Anne Ouyang (@anneouyang)
summary:
At the CUDA Mode IRL hackathon, @anneouyang and I tried this dream of ours as performance engineers: Can we get LLMs to go CUDA Mode 🧑‍💻 and write CUDA kernels?
Code → ⚙️ LLM → Optimized ⚡ Code, that goes brrrrrr 💨 on GPUs?
As much as I enjoyed learning and writing custom kernels for LLMs @cohere and for fun (making PRs to llm.c), it is incredibly hard to master CUDA knowledge 🥷 and super time-consuming 🐢 to write kernels for every new operators/hardware/input dimensions. 😵‍💫
Just as @karpathy talked about in his keynote, what if we can have a 🔮 “llm.c”, a set of custom kernels and optimized code, for any model architecture one like to optimize for?
Language models might be a piece of the puzzle 🧩 here. We designed KernelBench to see how far current LLMs can optimize PyTorch code with correct ✅ and performant 🏁 custom CUDA kernels.
We are surprised by some of the optimizations LLMs were able to generate, but also how much more room for improvement there could be!
A small step towards a future 🔭 where we can quickly create custom, performant software for any application.

Quoting @natfriedman
We did it! We tested 300 Bay Area foods for plastic chemicals. We found some interesting surprises.
Top 5 findings in our test results:
1. Our tests found plastic chemicals in 86% of all foods, with phthalates in 73% of the tested products and bisphenols in 22%. It's everywhere.
2. We detected phthalates in most baby foods and prenatal vitamins.
3. Hot foods which spend 45 minutes in takeout containers have 34% higher levels of plastic chemicals than the same dishes tested directly from the restaurant.
4. The 1950s Army rations we tested contained surprisingly high levels of plastic chemicals.
5. Almost every single one of the foods we tested are within both US FDA and EU EFSA regulations.

title: Anne Ouyang (@anneouyang)
summary:
a short bear case for nvidia
> NVIDIA’s main advantage is a software one (CUDA), not a hardware one (AMD has ~equally good GPU hardware)
> thanks to the rise of RL, LLM-based reasoning in auto-verified environments is really good now
> CUDA is essentially a layer of C code that runs python ML code on GPU
> this entails writing code that is fast (effectively utilizes the GPU) and correct (returns the right outputs)
> both speed and correctness are automatically verifiable
> people could (and will) use reinforcement learning to fine-tune LLMs to write these GPU kernels
> it’s entirely plausible that an incumbent could use AI to write CUDA
> it’s entirely plausible that an incumbent could use AI to write something better than CUDA
> nvidia has no moat

title: Anne Ouyang (@anneouyang)
summary:
another interesting work on LLM for kernel gen ft. KernelBench!
Quoting @SakanaAILabs
Introducing The AI CUDA Engineer: An agentic AI system that automates the production of highly optimized CUDA kernels.
The AI CUDA Engineer can produce highly optimized CUDA kernels, reaching 10-100x speedup over common machine learning operations in PyTorch. Our system is also able to produce highly optimized CUDA kernels that are much faster than existing CUDA kernels commonly used in production.
We believe that fundamentally, AI systems can and should be as resource-efficient as the human brain, and that the best path to achieve this efficiency is to use AI to make AI more efficient!
We are excited to publish our paper, The AI CUDA Engineer: Agentic CUDA Kernel Discovery, Optimization and Composition. We also release a dataset of over 17,000 verified CUDA kernels produced by The AI CUDA Engineer.
Paper:
Kernel Archive Webpage:
HuggingFace Dataset:
The AI CUDA Engineer utilizes evolutionary LLM-driven code optimization to autonomously improve the runtime of machine learning operations. Our system is not only able to convert PyTorch code into CUDA kernels, but through the use of evolution, it can also optimize the runtime performance of CUDA kernels, fuse multiple operations, and even discover novel solutions for writing efficient CUDA operations by learning from past innovations!
We believe The AI CUDA Engineer opens a new era of AI-driven acceleration of AI and automated inference time optimization.
We (@RobertTLange, @_Aaditya_Prasad, @Floating_Martin, @maxencefaldor, @yujin_tang, @hardmaru) are excited to continue Sakana AI's mission of leveraging AI to improve AI.

Title: Advice for a young investigator in the first and last days of the Anthropocene
Abstract: Within just a few years, it is likely that we will create AI systems that outperform the best humans on all intellectual tasks. This will have implications for your research and career! I will give practical advice, and concrete criteria to consider, when choosing research projects, and making professional decisions, in these last few years before AGI.
This is my current go-to academic talk. It's mostly targeted at early career scientists. It gets diverse and strong reactions. Let's try it here. Posting slides with speaker notes...
--
The title is a play on a very opinionated and pragmatic book by the nobel prize winner ramon y cajal, who is one of the founders of modern neuroscience.
To get you in the right mindset, on the right we have a plot of GDP vs time.
That is you, standing precariously on the top of that curve.
You are thinking to yourself -- I live in a pretty normal world.
Some things are going to change, but the future is going to look mostly like a linear extrapolation of the present.
And the plot should suggest that this may not be the right perspective on the future.
This plot by the way looks surprisingly similar even if you plot it on a log scale. We didn't stabilize on our current rate of growth until around 1950.

title: Anne Ouyang (@anneouyang)
summary:
Clock frequency directly affects performance. We were baffled why our matmul time depends on how many trials we run, and the answer turns out to be dynamic clocks. Even with clock locking, stability isn’t guaranteed. If the chosen SM frequency pushes the GPU past its power limit, the hardware will still throttle to stay within the cap. (4/9)
